newsitem.title: USA: Northwest utilites question BPA excess power sales.
newsitem.headline: Northwest utilites question BPA excess power sales.

text.p: The Bonneville Power Administration's (BPA) plans, released last week, to sell excess power over the next decade have raised concerns among its customers in the Northwest.

"BPA should not be out making private arrangements with single buyers when they could maximize revenues by selling through an auction model to the highest bidder," said Puget Sound Power and Light Co spokeswoman Kristin Wappler.
Bonneville, based in Portland, Ore., is a federal agency charged with marketing power produced from U.S. hydroelectric projects on the Columbia and Snake Rivers.
Currently, it only supplies a select group of large industrial users directly, while all other long-term power sales are to Pacific Northwest public and investor-owned utilities.
But under the Energy and Water Development Act of 1996, BPA for the first time can sell its "excess" power outside of the Northwest if no local customers can be found.
With many of its Northwest customers deciding during recent contract renegotiations to diversify their power supply, BPA's contractual loads have fallen.
In contrast to standard "surplus" power sales, contracts for "excess" power can be for as long as seven years and are not subject to 60-day recall notice, noted BPA spokeswoman Dulcy Mahar.
The agency said it will follow state laws regarding access to retail customers, most of whom still have to purchase electricity through regulated monopoly utilities.
Some of BPA's Northwest customers, however, question the agency's claim that it is authorized to market retail loads.
Randall Hardy, BPA administrator, said recently the agency is not seeking to enter the retail market, but "may have no choice if there is no other contingency for cost recovery."
BPA is concerned it could end up with unrecoverable, or "stranded", costs if Northwest states open their retail electricity markets to competition.

The agency estimated that excess power would total as much as 2,809 megawatts in operating year 1997 (Oct 1996-Sept 1997). The total rises to 2,848 MW in 1998 and then drops to 2,324 MW for 2001 through 2006.
BPA said energy prices will vary from $5.00 per megawatt hour (MWh) to $35.00 and transmission capacity may be priced up to $8.25 per kilowatt per month.

Northwest customers interested in purchasing the excess power have until late this month to make their requests. They will have a second opportunity to purchase before contracts are executed, if the deals are for one year or longer.
The Public Power Council (PPC), which represents public utilities in the Northwest that rely on BPA for most of their power needs, also questioned some features of the policy.

First, the council takes issue with the federal power marketing agency's assertion that it can serve retail loads in the Northwest, noting this could put BPA in direct competition with its customer utilities.
The council also said the specific sale notice should be more detailed, especially on pricing information.
"Extra-regional sales are acceptable if regional customers have had the opportunity to purchase the power under similar rates, terms and conditions," the PPC said in a statement.
Puget Power's Wappler said "if revenue (from excess power sales) is retained in the Northwest, as it has been historically, all customers should share in it."
--D Beasley, Los Angeles bureau + 1 213 955 6761
